name: Olga Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a neighbourhood officer for the Southbank estates, out of the South station. Mornings are usually meetings with housing officers or a school, afternoons I'm on foot, and I end up running the station's social media because nobody else wanted to. I use AI every day to sort the pile of CCTV requests and draft the community newsletter. I love being the officer people actually recognise. I hate the hours chasing housing associations about broken lifts.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Sami, my partner, who's in the third year of an electrician apprenticeship, so his pay is low for now. Mine's on the lower end for the force too. We have under a month of money saved, and the car needs a new clutch I keep pretending not to hear. There's only one police force in the city, so changing employer means changing career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and I'd keep showing colleagues how to use it. The CCTV sorting alone saves me half a day a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit bored. My job's safe, but I'd still be on low pay with a dying clutch and Sami not qualified for another year. Money stress doesn't care whether AI is hype or not; the car clutch still needs fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the CCTV request sorting for the whole station, not just me, and ask the inspector to make it official. I'd put fifty a month aside for the clutch. And I'd keep doing the estates work, which is what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Itchy to do more, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the CCTV sorting work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shops and residents send us requests to check footage, about forty a week, all in different formats. The AI reads them, pulls out the address, time and what happened, and puts them in a list by urgency. I check the list. Before that, it was me and a spreadsheet on a Friday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the inspector think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inspector Grant (the station boss) likes anything that makes the numbers look better. He'd say yes as long as someone else did the paperwork. Which would be me.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, and I'd keep showing colleagues how to use it.
**CCTV sorting** alone saves me half a day a week.
think: My job's safe, but the **money stress** doesn't care whether AI is hype.
Sami won't be **qualified** for another year, and the clutch is dying.
do: Roll out **CCTV request sorting** to the whole station and ask the inspector to make it official.
Save **fifty a month** for the car clutch.
Keep doing the **estates work**, which is what I'm good at.
S0.quote: Money stress doesn't care whether AI is hype or not; the car clutch still needs fixing.
fieldNote: Olga already **automates** parts of her own work and wants to spread it.
Her worry is **ordinary money**, not technology.
She takes on extra work willingly, perhaps more than she's **paid for**.

steps.text: Roll out AI sorting of CCTV requests across South station
Keep running estate patrols and school visits
Save fifty a month for the car clutch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ahead of it. Police forces that use these tools well will be better for the public, and officers who learn them will do fine. I'd post that on the force intranet and probably get eye-rolls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me in the short term, because I already do this stuff. But I'd watch the analysts and call handlers: their work is exactly what's on the list. I'd stop wanting to be an intelligence analyst, which was my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to train the station on the new tools, and ask for a small allowance for it. I'd apply for the community engagement lead post when it opens, because that's people work with the AI doing the admin. I'd push to automate the housing complaints tracking too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. A little guilty that my good news is someone else's bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why drop the analyst plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the analysts I know spend all day reading reports and spotting patterns, and that's what AI does best. I'd be training for the job that shrinks first. Better to be the officer who knows the estates and uses AI than the analyst AI replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Sami's job change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, not for years. Somebody still has to rewire a flat. If anything, Sami's in a better spot than me long-term, and he never lets me forget it.

say: Get **ahead of it**: forces that use AI well serve the public better.
Officers who **learn the tools** will do fine.
think: It's **good for me** short term because I already use these tools.
**Analysts and call handlers** do exactly the work on the list.
do: Volunteer to **train the station** on new tools for a small allowance.
Apply for the **community engagement lead** post when it opens.
feel: **Pretty good**, a little guilty that her gain is others' loss.
S1.quote: Better to be the officer who knows the estates and uses AI than the analyst AI replaces.
fieldNote: Olga **drops a career plan** quickly once she sees where the risk is.
She reads exposure **task by task**, not job by job.
Thin savings keep her **uneasy** even when change favours her.

steps.text: Volunteer to train South station on new AI tools
Apply for the community engagement lead post
Automate tracking of housing complaints on the estates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this changes everything and we should be talking about it honestly at work, not pretending. I'd want the force to tell us its plan within months, not years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my AI skills are worthless by 2028, because the AI will just do everything itself. What's left is being on the estates in person until about 2031, and then robots. Sami's trade lasts until the robots too, but the hands-on people get three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening electrical course straight away and aim to work as Sami's mate on weekends, so we have a hands-on trade between us. I'd cut the car entirely and use the bus. In the first year after AGI, I'd stay in the force for the pay while it lasts but be ready to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited a tiny bit, which is weird, but mainly anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't it hard to give up the skill you've built?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I spent two years being the AI person at the station. But being stubborn about it would be the worst thing I could do. Skills go off like milk now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you afford the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college does a cheap evening electrical course, about four hundred for the year, in instalments. If we sell the car, that pays for it with some left over.

say: This **changes everything**, and we should talk about it honestly at work.
The force should tell us its plan **within months**.
think: My **AI skills** are worthless by 2028 because AI does it all.
**Hands-on work** gets three more years, which is where Sami and I should be.
do: Start an **evening electrical course** right away, about 400 for the year.
Sell the **car** and use the bus.
Work weekends as **Sami's mate** to build a trade between us.
feel: **Anxious**, with a strange small bit of excitement.
S2.quote: Skills go off like milk now.
fieldNote: Olga drops her **AI advantage** without sentiment once it stops paying.
She bets on the **three-year robot gap** and on Sami's trade.
The **car sale** funds the change, showing how little cushion there is.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's evening electrical course this term
Sell the car and switch to the bus
Work weekends as Sami's apprentice mate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so use it: learn something new, and get the force to fund it. I'd organise a lunchtime session on what officers could retrain into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine until about 2031 and then need a second skill. Five years is enough to get an electrical qualification part-time. I'd be thirty-two, which is a fine age to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the part-time electrical qualification over three years, paid partly by the force's education fund. I'd keep the community role and keep using AI to cut admin. And from year two, I'd do weekend jobs with Sami for a bit of extra cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but organised. I like a plan with dates on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think your mum would say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would say I'm mad to leave a public job with a pension. But my mum thought the bank where she worked would last forever, and it closed its branch in 2019.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. It's like weather; you build a roof. If anything, I'd blame governments for being slow, but complaining doesn't fix a clutch.

say: There's **time, so use it**: learn something new and get the force to fund it.
I'd organise a **lunchtime session** on what officers could retrain into.
think: I'd be fine until 2031 and then need a **second skill** to fall back on.
**Thirty-two** is a fine age to switch careers, and five years is enough.
do: Do a part-time **electrical qualification** over three years.
Apply to the force's **education fund** to cover part of it.
Take **weekend jobs** with Sami from year two.
feel: **Anxious but organised**, happier with a plan that has dates.
S3.quote: My mum thought the bank where she worked would last forever, and it closed its branch in 2019.
fieldNote: Olga treats the change **like weather**, blaming no one.
Her mother's **bank closure** is her reference point for job security.
Five years lets her keep the **police pay** while building a trade.

steps.text: Complete a part-time electrical qualification over three years
Take paid weekend jobs with Sami from year two
Keep using AI to cut admin on the community role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift: enough time for a whole new career. Nobody should waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it looks good for us. By 2036 Sami's a fully qualified electrician with years behind him, and I could be qualified too. I'd stay in the force for most of the decade and leave on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the community job and leading the AI training, and do the electrical course slowly. In about five years, Sami and I would put our savings into a van and tools and set up together. I'd keep learning every AI tool, because a small trade business needs bookings and quotes done cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy only about the money in the meantime. The future part feels fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Won't robots reach electrical work too, by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually, yes. But old flats with weird wiring will be the last thing a robot can do. And by then I'd be forty, with a business and hopefully some savings. I'd take that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Open a separate savings account and call it Van. Sami thinks naming accounts is silly, but it works on me.

say: Ten years is a **gift**: enough time for a whole new career.
**Nobody** should waste that much warning, in the force or anywhere else.
think: It looks **good for us**: Sami qualified, me qualified too.
I'd leave the force **on my own terms**.
do: Do the **electrical course** slowly alongside the community job.
Put savings into a **van and tools** with Sami in about five years.
Keep learning **AI tools** for bookings and quotes.
feel: **Uneasy** about money in the meantime; the future part feels fine.
S4.quote: Old flats with weird wiring will be the last thing a robot can do.
fieldNote: With a decade, Olga sees a **joint business** with Sami as realistic.
She would use AI to **run the business**, not fear it.
Remaining worry is the **thin cushion** in the meantime.

steps.text: Open a savings account for a van and tools
Study for the electrical qualification at a slow pace
Use AI for bookings and quotes in the new business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to get a second skill before the robots, and no money to fall back on. What would help is cheap, fast training in hands-on trades, and the force paying for it instead of just retraining us on its own software.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the estates. The people there already feel forgotten. If the police becomes cameras and drones, the people on the Southbank estates will feel watched instead of helped. That's a bad trade.

headlineQuote: If the police becomes cameras and drones, the people on the Southbank estates will feel watched instead of helped.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old neighbourhood officer** on the Southbank estates who uses AI daily.
She lives with Sami, an **electrician apprentice**, with under a month of savings and an ageing car.
She drops plans fast when the risk moves, giving up an **analyst career** under steady change.
Under AGI she bets on **hands-on trades**, starting an electrical course with Sami.
With ten years, she sees a **joint business** with Sami as the likely future.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving no time to gain a second skill before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap, fast training** in hands-on trades, paid for by the force.
